extracted.intended_audience: editors, journal staff, authors, and peer reviewers of biomedical/medical journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating, implementing, and enforcing conflict-of-interest (COI) policies for peer-reviewed medical journals, covering definitions, types of interests, disclosure processes, and management actions for authors, reviewers, and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear definition the journal uses as to what is conflict of interest and who is captured in the definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample definition provided: 'conflict of interest exists when a participant in the publication process (author, peer reviewer or editor) has a competing interest that could unduly influence (or be reasonably seen to do so) his or her responsibilities in the publication process (submission of manuscripts, peer review, editorial decisions, and communication between authors, reviewers and editors)'. Journals should state explicitly who (authors, reviewers, editors, others) are covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of competing interests (must be declared)
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear statement of examples of the types of competing interests (and their definitions) the journal says must be declared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WAME lists examples that should be included (but not limited to): (I) Financial ties; (II) Academic commitments; (III) Personal relationships; (IV) Political or religious beliefs; (V) Institutional affiliations. The policy should articulate examples and definitions and recognize that multiple competing interests can coexist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaring conflicts of interest (what, when, to whom, format, consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear statements on: (I) what is to be declared, when and to whom; (II) format for declaration; (III) a journal’s role in asking additional questions or seeking clarification about disclosures; and, (IV) consequences for failing to disclose before or after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals rely on self-declaration, so the policy should ask about COI in a way that maximizes truthful reporting. Provide templates/format (e.g., ICMJE uniform format), specify timing (submission, revision, post-publication updates), who receives declarations, and list potential consequences (investigation, corrections, retractions, rejection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing conflict of interests (how the journal will act)
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear statement on how conflict of interest will be managed by the journal, including the position that all relevant COI disclosures (or the declaration of no COI) will be published with the article and clarity about what COI situations will result in a manuscript not being considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe specific management measures (e.g., exclusion from review/decision-making, editorial oversight, independent review). Make rules known to all participants. Acknowledge that journals use various rules and should state which apply. Specify circumstances that may lead to rejection or special handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish disclosures with every article (transparency requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should publish with every article all relevant author disclosures so readers have transparency about conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make disclosures visible in the article record (e.g., disclosure statement, footnote). Publishing disclosures is emphasized as necessary for reader trust; failure to publish disclosures undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors’ responsibility to investigate and act on undisclosed COI
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors have a responsibility for investigating, and if relevant acting, if competing interests surface after a manuscript is submitted or published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat allegations of failure to declare seriously. Investigative actions may include requesting clarification, issuing corrections, expressions of concern, or retractions. The policy should state procedures for post-publication allegations and follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-financial conflicts (expand scope beyond financial ties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies should move beyond just financial COI to include non-financial conflicts such as clinical income, intellectual passion, personal relationships, political or religious beliefs, and institutional affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide definitions and examples of non-financial interests (e.g., physicians whose clinical income depends on a technology; intellectual commitments to a position). Encourage journals to require disclosure of these interests and explain how they might bias judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full written disclosure as the backbone but not a complete remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Full written disclosure is essential ('the backbone of managing conflicts') because without it nothing else is possible, but disclosure alone is an imperfect remedy and editors must still determine whether a conflict impairs objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require comprehensive, written disclosures at submission and updates when circumstances change. However, include guidance that editors should assess disclosed interests' potential impact and take management actions beyond mere publication of disclosures when necessary (e.g., reject, limit role, independent review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal-specific standards, accessibility, and context sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: WAME encourages journals to establish their own operational definitions and standards for COI, recognizing differences in context, resources, and culture; journals should make these policies readily accessible to everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow flexibility for journals to set thresholds and actions appropriate to their discipline and setting. Publish the journal’s COI policy prominently (website, instructions for authors). Warn against overly expansive lists that could paralyze peer review; editors must make context-sensitive judgments about the strength of conflicts.
